title_en: What adding an album version does to first-week sales
title_kr: 버전을 하나 더 내면 초동은 얼마나 오르나
subtitle_en: Sales do not rise in proportion to versions — going from 3 to 4 versions goes with about 10% more first-week sales, and doubling the versions with about 25% more, not 100%.
body_en: It is true that albums with more versions sell more: albums with 2 versions typically sell about 27,000 copies in their first week, albums with 16 or more sell close to a million. But that is a trap. Companies decide how many versions to make after looking at how popular the artist already is — a big fandom gets a big set, a small one gets two versions. So comparing albums with many versions to albums with few mostly compares popular artists to less popular ones, and tells you nothing about what the versions themselves do. The fair test is to follow one artist and see what changes when their version count changes. Done that way, the effect is real but small. Say the last album had 3 versions. Albums that went from 3 to 4 versions sold about 10% more than we would otherwise expect; 3 to 5, about 18% more; 3 to 6 — double — about 25% more, not 100%. The table gives the same for other starting points; the fewer versions you started with, the more each extra one is worth, and albums that cut versions sold less by about the same amount in reverse. This is a correlation, not a cause: a company that expects a strong comeback may also add versions.
table_md:
| Versions last time | +1 version | +2 versions | +3 versions | −1 version |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | +25% | +42% | +56% | — |
| 2 | +14% | +25% | +34% | −20% |
| 3 | +10% | +18% | +25% | −12% |
| 4 | +7% | +14% | +20% | −9% |
| 5 | +6% | +11% | +16% | −7% |
| 6 | +5% | +10% | +14% | −6% |
(Same artist, same album type, same gap — only the version count changes. Averages over artists of all sizes.)

title_en: The last album already tells you most of the next one
title_kr: 전작 초동이 다음 앨범의 대부분을 말해준다
subtitle_en: Know one number — last comeback's first week — and you know most of what can be known: it accounts for about 79% of the differences between albums.
body_en: If you know only one thing about an artist — how many copies their previous comeback sold in its first week — you already know most of what the next one will do: that single number accounts for about 79% of the differences between albums. Everything else we could gather on top of it — album type, how many versions, how the fandom has been growing, how long the break was, where the artist came from — adds only a little, taking it to about 85%. 79% is not an accuracy score. Even with everything included, our guesses are still typically off by about 46%; see the About page.

title_en: The whole market swings year to year
subtitle_en: How much the typical comeback grew over the same artist's previous album swung from +39% in 2020 to 0% in 2024: about +30% a year in 2019–2022, +10% in 2023, flat since 2024.
body_en: K-pop album sales don't just move artist by artist; the whole market moves together, and the swing is large. From 2019 to 2022 a typical comeback sold 27% to 39% more than the same artist's previous album; in 2023 that fell to +10%, and in 2024, 2025 and 2026 so far the typical comeback has been flat (0%, −2%, +2%). Total sales tell the same story from the top: a record 119 million copies in 2023, then −17% in 2024, the first decline in ten years. For a forecast made months ahead this matters: when the market turns, our forecasts for every album are off in the same direction by roughly 15%, and no information about an individual artist warns you in advance. Three years show the pattern, and here is our reading of each. 2020: concerts stopped, fan spending moved into albums, and the typical comeback jumped 39% over its predecessor. 2023: the total hit its all-time high on the strength of a few huge groups, while the typical album grew only 10% — the market was already cooling underneath the headline. 2024: the total fell 17% as overseas group-buying pulled back, and the typical comeback stopped growing at all. These readings fit the timing, but the sales figures alone cannot prove what caused each swing.

title_en: The longer the silence, the smaller the first week
subtitle_en: The typical comeback arrives about eight and a half months after the previous album. Comebacks one to two years after the last album sold about 6% less than comebacks six to twelve months after; four years or more, about 13% less.
body_en: 50% of the comebacks in our data arrive within 8.5 months of the previous album, and the most common gap is six to twelve months. We use that group as the baseline: what an album of the same artist size, the same type, the same change in versions and the same recent Instagram growth would sell if it came back six to twelve months after the last one. Measured against that baseline, comebacks within six months sold about 5% more (416 albums), those after one to two years about 6% less (315), two to four years about 8% less (160), and four years or more about 13% less (64). Read the raw numbers without that adjustment and a long silence looks harmless, even good: albums four or more years after the last one typically sold 35% more than the previous album. That is a trick of who gets to come back. Comebacks after military service, and acts a company still believed in after a long break, are the ones we see; the acts that stopped selling simply never released again. This is a pattern in past sales, not proof that the gap itself is what shrinks the first week.

title_en: K-pop albums became a fan-only market: the first week is now 84% of total sales
subtitle_en: In 2015 the first week was about 26% of an album's total sales in Korea. In 2025 it was 84%, and 2026 so far is higher still.
body_en: Add up all first-week sales in our data and divide by everything those same albums ever sold in Korea: about 26% in 2015, 44% in 2019, 62% in 2022, 84% in 2025. Almost nothing sells after week one any more. The shift is strongest for mid-size and big acts, whose first week is now over 90% of the total, and weakest for the smallest acts, at about 50% — their albums still trickle out to the general public afterwards. One likely reason is how the market now works: fan-sign slots go to pre-orders, so a large share of what a fandom will ever spend on an album is committed before release and lands in the first week. The demand that used to be released gradually over the following months is now pulled forward into week one, and total sales barely grow after it. Three other series move the same way: the first day's share of the first week rose from 23% (2016) to about 46% (2022–2026); the typical album went from 1 version to 4; the typical price rose from 12,600 to 19,300 won. The market's growth was not new listeners buying CDs — it was existing fans buying more copies, more versions, earlier. That is why this site forecasts the first week and not total sales: after week one, there is little left to forecast. The figures show the shift; the reasons given above are likely ones, not proven.

title_en: The typical fan stays for about three years
subtitle_en: Every comeback wins a new group of fans, and each group's support tapers on the albums that follow. The fan life cycle that best fits the data: about 50% of each group is gone after roughly two years.
body_en: Think of every comeback as winning a new group of fans. Each group supports the album that won them the most, and a little less on each album after that, as some of them drift away. An artist's first-week sales are what all these groups — the newest and the older ones — are still putting in, stacked together. We asked the data how fast a group fades, and the answer is about 50% every two years, which means the typical fan stays for about three years. Three things follow. In this picture, sales rise only while each new group outweighs the fading of the older ones. Once new groups get small, sales fall even though nothing went wrong, falling about 50% every two years. And an act whose sales hold steady for years is not keeping the same fans; it is replacing the ones who leave at about the rate they leave. That fits what fans say about themselves (two to three years), and it fits the supply side: the average Korean idol group is active for about four years, and about 45% are gone within three. This is an average, not a rule for any one fan — some stay a decade, many leave within a year.

title_en: Full album, mini, single, repackage: how they compare
subtitle_en: Compared with a mini album by the same artist, a full album sells about 15% more, a single album about 23% less, and a repackage about 47% less.
body_en: 50% of the artists in our data have never released a full album, so the mini album is the natural yardstick. To keep rising and falling artists on an equal footing, we compared each full album with the mini album just before it and the mini album just after it. A full album typically sells about 10–20% more than those two minis, and it beat them in 65% of cases. Our forecast uses the same yardstick: once an artist's size, fan growth and gap are accounted for, a full album comes in about 15% above a mini album, a single album about 23% below, and a repackage about 47% below. The full-album bump is not the same for everyone. For artists whose last album sold between 50,000 and 500,000 copies it is about 25%; for smaller artists and for the very biggest we cannot tell whether there is any bump at all, partly because they release too few full albums for us to be sure. Girl groups seem to get a bigger full-album bump than boy groups, about 33% against 9%, but with only 37 girl-group full albums in our data we cannot be sure of that difference. A single album sells about 20–35% less than a mini at every size. A repackage is the same album issued again with a few new songs about ten weeks later. Looked at raw, without adjusting for anything, a repackage typically sells 56% of the original, close to the 47% drop above. This describes what happened; it does not mean that choosing one type causes the difference.

title_en: A drop in sales is a one-off, not a trend
title_kr: 초동 하락은 한 번의 사건이지 추세가 아니다
subtitle_en: After an album falls by more than 20%, the chance that the next one falls again is 23%, about the same as for any album (25%). The lost ground usually stays lost, but the slide does not continue.
body_en: When an album sells clearly less than the one before, it is tempting to draw a line through the two points and expect every future comeback to fall by the same amount. The data does not support that. We looked at 1,663 comebacks where we knew whether the previous album had risen or fallen. After an album fell by more than 20%, the next album fell by more than 20% again in 23% of cases, rose by more than 25% in 53%, and landed in between in 25%. That is the same spread as after any album: across all comebacks, 25% fall by more than 20%. The same holds for boy groups, girl groups and soloists, for big and small artists, and for new and long-running acts. Even after two drops in a row, the third album rose more often than it fell. What a drop does do is move the starting point. After a fall of 20–40%, the next album typically sells about the same as the album that fell, so the lost ground usually stays lost. So read a bad first week as a step down to a new level, not as the first step of a staircase. One caution: artists whose sales fall very hard sometimes never release the next album, so we can only see the ones who came back. This is a pattern in past sales, not proof of what causes what.

title_en: Boy groups hold on to their sales best; soloists swing the most
title_kr: 보이그룹은 초동을 가장 잘 지키고, 솔로는 가장 크게 흔들린다
subtitle_en: After a boy-group album, the next one loses no more than 20% of the first-week sales in 80% of cases; for a girl group that happens in 75% of cases, for a soloist in about 60%.
body_en: Fans often say that boy-group fans stay longer and girl-group fans move on faster, and the sales bear that out, though the gap is modest. Take every album and ask whether the next one kept at least 80% of its first-week sales. For boy groups the answer is yes 80% of the time, for girl groups 75% of the time. Two albums on, boy groups are still holding that level 82% of the time and girl groups 73% of the time. Soloists do worse. A soloist's next album keeps at least 80% of the previous one only about 60% of the time, and two albums on a male soloist is holding the level only about 52% of the time. Female soloists swing the most: 42% of their albums either double or halve compared with the last one. So a soloist's big album is more often a one-off, and a boy group's big album is more often a new floor. These are descriptions of what happened, not causes.

title_en: Release weekday does not affect first-week sales; it affects which charts an album lands on
title_kr: 발매 요일은 초동에 영향이 없다, 영향을 받는 것은 다른 차트다
subtitle_en: Albums released on any weekday sell about the same relative to the artist's last album. The weekday matters for weekly charts that close on a fixed day, not for the seven-day first-week count.
body_en: Comebacks released on a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday typically sold 15% to 26% more than the artist's previous album, with no order to the days, and the differences are no bigger than chance alone would produce. Adding the weekday to our forecast does not make it any better. The reason is simple: the first week is a rolling seven-day window that starts on the release day, so every album gets its full seven days. The weekday does matter for charts that close on a fixed day of the week: an album released late in a chart week has only a few days counted before that chart closes, so its first chart position can look weaker even though its first-week total is unaffected. Weekend releases are too rare in our data to say anything about them.

title_en: Follower count tells you how big an artist is; follower growth tells you where they are going
title_kr: 팔로워 수는 크기를, 팔로워 증가 속도는 방향을 말해준다
subtitle_en: Without sales history, follower count is the single most useful number. Once you know the last album, the follower count adds nothing new — it is measuring the same thing. How fast the fanbase grew during the gap still adds something: the fastest-growing 25% of artists sold 34% more than their last album, the slowest 25% about the same (0%).
body_en: We track each artist's Instagram followers monthly. The number of followers is a good measure of how big an artist is: when we do not know an artist's previous sales, adding follower count is the single biggest improvement we can make, and an artist with ten times the followers sells about five times as many copies. But the previous album already measures size, and measures it better. Once the last album is in the picture, follower count adds nothing new — it is measuring the same thing. What still adds something is how fast the fanbase is growing, measured as followers gained per month divided by followers already held. Among the 1,240 comebacks with this data, the 25% of artists whose followers grew slowest during the gap typically sold about the same as their previous album (0%), and 50% of them rose. The 25% that grew fastest typically sold 34% more, and 75% of them rose. That still holds after everything else we know is taken into account: with the last album, album type, versions and gap already accounted for, the fastest-growing 25% still come in about 17% above what we would otherwise expect. This helps predict sales, but it is not proof that follower growth causes them: growth and sales tend to rise for the same reasons.

title_en: Messy data is not why forecasts miss: copying mistakes explain about 1% of the error
title_kr: 예측이 빗나가는 건 데이터 오류 때문이 아니다: 옮겨 적기 실수는 오차의 약 1%
subtitle_en: We checked the first-week figures we forecast against the official counts. Almost all matched exactly, and the few wrong ones explain about 1% of our error. Our misses are real differences in what albums sold.
body_en: A fair objection to any sales model is that the numbers themselves are unreliable. We can measure how unreliable they are. We checked 196 of the albums we forecast against the official first-week counts. 190 of them matched to within 0.05%, and the 5 that did not were copying mistakes we have since fixed. Even counted before the fix, those wrong figures explain under 6% of our forecast error on the checked albums, and about 1% across all 1,140 albums we scored, in a measure where big misses weigh more than small ones. Our forecast misses by a typical 46%, so the rest of each miss is a real difference between what the album sold and what we expected, not a problem with the sales numbers. The same is true between two near-identical albums by the same artist, which differ by about 38% for no visible reason.
